explain.say: Every chip in your phone starts as sand. Purified silicon is a poor conductor, but add a pinch of the right impurity and it conducts on demand. That pinch, called doping, is the trick behind every diode, transistor and solar panel. On the board, silicon is sorted three ways: pure, n-type and p-type.

explain.say: Pure silicon first. Each atom has four outer electrons and shares them in four bonds with its neighbours, a neat crystal. To break free and carry current, an electron needs about 1.1 electronvolts of energy, called the band gap. At room temperature only about 10 billion electrons per cubic centimetre manage it, among 50 thousand billion billion atoms. Is pure silicon a good conductor, then?

explain.say: No, a poor one. Now add phosphorus, which has five outer electrons. Four join the bonds and the fifth is left loose, free to wander. Silicon doped this way is n-type, for negative, because its majority carriers are electrons. Dope 1 atom in 5 million and you get a million times more free electrons than pure silicon. Is the doped crystal now electrically charged?

explain.say: No, it stays neutral, since each phosphorus nucleus keeps an extra proton. Now boron, with only three outer electrons. It leaves one bond missing an electron, a gap called a hole. A neighbour's electron can hop in, so the hole moves the other way, behaving like a positive charge. That is p-type silicon, where holes are the majority carriers. Which way does a hole drift in an electric field?

explain.say: With the field, like a positive charge. Superb! Put p-type and n-type side by side and you get a p-n junction, the heart of the diode, which is our next lesson. Wow fact: chip makers place dopant atoms so precisely that some layers in a modern transistor are only a few atoms thick. Challenge: arsenic has five outer electrons. Is arsenic-doped silicon n-type or p-type?

faq.a: Doping is adding a tiny, controlled amount of impurity atoms to a pure semiconductor to change its conductivity. Even 1 atom in millions raises it enormously.
Silicon doped with atoms that have five outer electrons, such as phosphorus or arsenic. The spare electrons are free to move, so electrons are the majority carriers.

faq.q: What is a hole in a semiconductor?
faq.a: A hole is a missing electron in a bond. Neighbouring electrons can hop into it, so the hole moves through the crystal and acts like a positive charge.

faq.q: What is the band gap of silicon?
faq.a: About 1.12 electronvolts at room temperature. It is the energy an electron needs to break free of its bond and carry current.
No. Each dopant atom brings exactly as many protons as electrons, so the crystal stays neutral overall. Only the number of mobile carriers changes.
asks: Does n-type silicon have a negative charge?

facts: Pure silicon at room temperature has only about 10 billion free electrons per cubic centimetre.
Phosphorus and arsenic are common donor dopants for silicon, and boron is the common acceptor.

quiz.say: Silicon doped with boron is which type?
quiz.why: Boron has three outer electrons, so it leaves holes, which are positive carriers.

wrong.1: n-type needs a dopant with five outer electrons, like phosphorus.
wrong.2: Any deliberate dopant makes the silicon extrinsic, not intrinsic.

quiz.say: Silicon has an intrinsic carrier concentration of 10 to the 10 per cubic centimetre, and is doped with 10 to the 16 donors. What is the hole concentration?
quiz.show: Silicon has n_i = 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ and is doped with 10¹⁶ donors per cm³. What is the hole concentration?
quiz.why: n times p equals n i squared, so p is 10 to the 20 over 10 to the 16, which is 10 to the 4.

wrong.1: That is the pure-silicon value; doping with donors pushes the holes far below it.
wrong.2: That is the electron concentration, the majority carriers.
